newsitem.title: USA: Turkey denies overflying Cyprus, U.S. says.
newsitem.headline: Turkey denies overflying Cyprus, U.S. says.

text.p: Turkey denied to U.S. officials charges by the government of Cyprus that its warplanes violated Cypriot airspace Tuesday, the State Department said.
The Greek Cypriot government said earlier it would protest to the United Nations over what it said was the violation by three Turkish F-4 planes.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said the Cypriot government had told the U.S. embassy in Nicosia of the alleged violation, but Turkey had denied it.
"The Turkish government has told us that Turkish planes were in the area, but they did not violate Cypriot airspace," he said.
"Such flights, if they did occur, would in fact be a deviation from Turkey's unilateral decision to suspend military overflights over Cyprus," Burns told reporters.

Burns said that, according to the Cypriot complaint, the F-4s had entered Cypriot airspace near Kyrenia, in the Turkish Cypriot sector of the island, and had penetrated at least three nautical miles inland before leaving.
Burns said unilateral decisions two months ago by Cyprus and Turkey to suspend overflights were "very valuable" and Washington hoped they would be continued.

Cyprus spokesman Manolis Christofides said his government would not reverse its decision to suspend Greek military flights over the divided island. The flights were carried out under a defence pact between the governments of Greece and Cyprus. The Greek Cypriots do not have an airforce.

The suspension was part of moves to prepare for long-awaited talks next month between the leaders of the Greek and Turkish Cypriot communities on how to reunite the island, divided after a Turkish invasion in 1974.
